claim: E. coli were selected for faster migration through a porous environment, a process which depends on both motility and growth.
source: we select Escherichia coli for faster migration through a porous environment, a process which depends on both motility and growth.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and demonstrated through the experimental design described in the manuscript.

claim: A trade-off between swimming speed and growth rate constrains the evolution of faster migration.
source: We find that a trade-off between swimming speed and growth rate constrains the evolution of faster migration.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing opposing changes in swimming speed and growth rate across different media conditions.

claim: Evolving faster migration in rich medium results in slow growth and fast swimming.
source: Evolving faster migration in rich medium results in slow growth and fast swimming
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by measurements shown in Figure 3g and Figure 3e showing decreased growth rate and increased swimming speed in rich medium evolved strains.

claim: Evolution in minimal medium results in fast growth and slow swimming.
source: while evolution in minimal medium results in fast growth and slow swimming.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 3h and Figure 3f showing increased growth rate and decreased swimming speed in minimal medium evolved strains.

claim: In each condition parallel genomic evolution drives adaptation through different mutations.
source: In each condition parallel genomic evolution drives adaptation through different mutations.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by whole genome sequencing data shown in Figure 5, which reveals different mutations in rich versus minimal medium conditions.

claim: The trade-off is mediated by antagonistic pleiotropy through mutations that affect negative regulation.
source: We show that the trade-off is mediated by antagonistic pleiotropy through mutations that affect negative regulation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by genetic reconstruction experiments showing that single mutations (clpXE185* and galSL22R) affect both traits in opposite directions.

claim: The genetic capacity of an organism to vary traits can qualitatively depend on its environment, which in turn alters its evolutionary trajectory.
source: A model of the evolutionary process shows that the genetic capacity of an organism to vary traits can qualitatively depend on its environment, which in turn alters its evolutionary trajectory.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the evolutionary model presented in Figure 6 and related analysis.

claim: E. coli inoculated at the center of a low viscosity agar plate consume nutrients locally, creating a spatial nutrient gradient which drives chemotaxis through the porous agar matrix.
source: E. coli inoculated at the center of a low viscosity agar plate consume nutrients locally, creating a spatial nutrient gradient which drives chemotaxis through the porous agar matrix (Righetti et al., 1981; Maaloum et al., 1998) and subsequent nutrient consumption (Adler, 1966; Wolfe and Berg, 1989; Croze et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The outermost edge of the expanding colony is driven by both growth and motility.
source: As a result, the outermost edge of the expanding colony is driven by both growth and motility (Koster et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: 10 to 12 generations occurred in each round of selection in rich medium.
source: We estimated that 10 to 12 generations occurred in each round of selection.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on measurements of cell numbers before and after each round.

claim: Prolonged growth in well mixed liquid medium for 200 generations resulted in only a 3.5% increase in the rate of migration.
source: We observed only a 3.5% increase in the rate of migration
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Selection performed on spatially structured populations results in more rapid adaptation for fast migration than growth in well mixed conditions.
source: demonstrating that selection performed on spatially structured populations results in more rapid adaptation for fast migration than growth in well mixed conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by comparing migration rate evolution in structured versus well-mixed conditions.

claim: Less than 10 generations occurred per round of selection in minimal medium.
source: We therefore take this as an upper bound and conclude that the 10 round selection experiment includes <100 generations.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on measurements of cell numbers.

claim: Increases in run speed and growth rate have the largest impact on migration rate according to the reaction-diffusion model.
source: We found that increases in run speed (|vr|) and growth rate (kg) had the largest impact on s (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated by simulations shown in Figure 2.

claim: Only small gains in migration rate can be achieved through increases in tumble frequency according to the model.
source: Consistent with previous reports, our model indicates that only small gains in migration rate can be achieved through increases in tumble frequency (Wolfe and Berg, 1989) (∼10%, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by simulations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and a citation.

claim: Run durations declined over the course of selection in both rich and minimal media.
source: Figure 3a–b shows that run durations declined over the course of selection in both rich and minimal media.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3a-b.

claim: Evolved strains exhibited a reduction in the probability of executing long runs.
source: These distributions show that the evolved strains exhibited a reduction in the probability of executing long runs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3a-b.

claim: Tumble duration decreased in rich medium and increased in minimal medium during evolution.
source: We observed opposite trends for tumble duration, with decreasing tumble duration in rich medium and increasing duration in minimal medium (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: An increase in tumble frequency was observed in both rich and minimal media conditions.
source: In both conditions, we observe an increase in the tumble frequency.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3c-d.

claim: Mutants with increased tumble frequencies have faster migration rates through agar, likely due to tumbles freeing cells from being trapped in the agar.
source: This is expected since previous studies showed that mutants with increased tumble frequencies have faster migration rates through agar, likely due to tumbles freeing cells from being trapped in the agar (Wolfe and Berg, 1989).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: The increase in run speed in rich medium was reproducible across independent evolution experiments.
source: Tracking strains isolated after 15 rounds from independent selection experiments (replicates 3 and 4, Figure 1c) showed that this increase in run speed was reproducible across independent evolution experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: A 50% reduction in run speed was observed in strains evolved in minimal media.
source: Surprisingly, when we performed single-cell tracking for strains evolved in minimal media we observed the opposite trend. In these conditions we observed a 50% reduction in run speed (Figure 3f).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3f.

claim: The reduction in run speed in minimal medium was reproducible across independently evolved strains.
source: Again, we found that this result was reproducible across independently evolved strains (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: A decline of about 10% in the maximum growth rate was observed with selection in rich medium.
source: We observed a decline of about 10% in the maximum growth rate with selection in rich medium
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3g.

claim: A three-fold increase in the maximum growth rate was observed after 10 rounds of selection in minimal medium.
source: and a three-fold increase in the maximum growth rate after 10 rounds of selection in minimal medium (Figure 3g-h).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3h.

claim: Changes in growth rate are reproducible across independently evolved strains in both environmental conditions.
source: We found that these changes in growth rate are reproducible across independently evolved strains in both environmental conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The reaction-diffusion model qualitatively recapitulated the increase in front migration rate observed experimentally.
source: We found that the model qualitatively recapitulated the increase in front migration rate that we observed experimentally (Tables 3,4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Tables 3-4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is a trade-off between run speed and growth rate in E. coli which constrains the evolution of faster migration through low viscosity agar.
source: We conclude that there is a trade-off between run speed and growth rate in E. coli which constrains the evolution of faster migration through low viscosity agar.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The evolved phenotypes lie near a Pareto frontier in the phenotypic space of run speed and growth rate.
source: The curves in Figure 4a–b show that the evolved phenotypes lie near a Pareto frontier in the phenotypic space of run speed and growth rate.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4.

claim: Parallel evolution was observed across replicate selection experiments in rich medium, with a mutation in clpX (E185*) and an intergenic single base pair deletion both rising to fixation within approximately 5 rounds of selection.
source: In the rich medium experiment we observed parallel evolution across replicate selection experiments, with a mutation in clpX (E185*) and an intergenic single base pair deletion both rising to fixation within approximately 5 rounds of selection.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Mutations in clpX alter flhDC expression and motility.
source: A previous study showed that mutations in clpX alter flhDC expression and motility (Girgis et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: The clpXE185* mutation converted position 185 from glutamic acid to a stop codon in the 424 residue ClpX protein.
source: We therefore focused attention on the mutation in clpX, which converted position 185 from glutamic acid to a stop codon in the 424 residue ClpX protein.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on sequencing data.

claim: ClpX is the specificity subunit of the ClpX-ClpP serine protease.
source: ClpX is the specificity subunit of the ClpX-ClpP serine protease.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and represents established knowledge.

claim: ClpX forms a homohexamer that consumes ATP to unfold and translocate target proteins to the ClpP peptidase.
source: ClpX forms a homohexamer that consumes ATP to unfold and translocate target proteins to the ClpP peptidase (Baker and Sauer, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: The ClpXP protease has many targets in the cell including FlhDC, the master regulator of flagellar biosynthesis.
source: The ClpXP protease has many targets in the cell including FlhDC, the master regulator of flagellar biosynthesis (Tomoyasu et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: The clpXE185* mutation resulted in a statistically significant increase in run speed relative to founder (24.2 μm s−1 compared to 18.7 μm s−1).
source: We also found that clpXE185* resulted in a statistically significant increase in run speed relative to founder (24.2 μm s−1 compared to 18.7 μm s−1, p< 10-10).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on single-cell tracking measurements.

claim: The stop codon mutation in clpX has a more subtle effect on the enzyme's function than a simple loss of function.
source: suggesting that the stop codon mutation we observe has a more subtle effect on the enzyme's function than a simple loss of function.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and inferred from comparing the clpXE185* mutant phenotype to the clpX knockout phenotype.

claim: The intergenic single base pair deletion is neutral.
source: These results suggest that this intergenic mutation is neutral.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on reconstruction experiments showing no phenotypic effects.

claim: The clpX mutation drives faster front migration through increasing run speed, despite decreasing growth rate.
source: We conclude that the clpX mutation observed in all four replicate experiments drives faster front migration through increasing run speed, despite decreasing growth rate.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by phenotypic measurements of the reconstructed mutant.

claim: The trade-off between growth rate and swimming speed is driven by antagonistic pleiotropy.
source: Since the mutant exhibits both faster swimming and slower growth rate relative to founder we conclude that the trade-off between growth rate and swimming speed is driven by antagonistic pleiotropy (Cooper and Lenski, 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the observation that single mutations affect both traits in opposite directions.

claim: Mutations in the transcriptional regulator galS fixed in just five rounds in all minimal medium experiments.
source: In all experiments, we observed mutations in the transcriptional regulator galS which fixed in just five rounds.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The galSL22R mutation occurs in the highly conserved N-terminal helix-turn-helix DNA binding region of the protein.
source: The coding mutation we observe occurs in the highly conserved N-terminal helix-turn-helix DNA binding region of this protein
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on knowledge of protein structure.

claim: The galSL22R mutation is expected to alter the expression of the gal regulon.
source: we therefore expect that this mutation alters the expression of the gal regulon (Weickert and Adhya, 1992).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation and inference from the mutation location.

claim: The galSL22R mutation reduced the mean swimming speed relative to founder by approximately 15%.
source: Further, this mutation reduced the mean swimming speed relative to founder by approximately 15% (Figure 4b, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4b and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The galSL22R mutation alone drives faster growth and slower swimming.
source: Therefore, as shown in Figure 4b, we conclude that galSL22R alone drives faster growth and slower swimming.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4b.

claim: In minimal medium, the trade-off is governed by antagonistic pleiotropy.
source: As with the rich medium condition, this trade-off is governed by antagonistic pleiotropy.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the observation that the galSL22R mutation affects both traits in opposite directions.

claim: The direction of phenotypic evolution in rich medium agreed well with experimental observations when σ|υ~r|/σkg~ ≥ 1 for ρ < −0.1.
source: We found that the direction of phenotypic evolution in rich medium agreed well with our experimental observations so long as σ|υ~r|/σkg~≥1 for ρ<−0.1.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on modeling analysis.

claim: The observed phenotypic evolution in rich medium is consistent with a genetic variance in run speed that is no smaller than the genetic variance in growth rate.
source: This implies that our observed phenotypic evolution is consistent with a genetic variance in run speed that is no smaller than the genetic variance in growth rate (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: In minimal medium, the model predicts the direction of observed phenotypic evolution only if σ|υ~r|/σkg~ ≲ 0.3 for ρ < −0.1.
source: In contrast, in minimal medium the model predicts the direction of observed phenotypic evolution only if σ|υ~r|/σkg~≲0.3 for ρ<−0.1.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on modeling analysis.

claim: The observed phenotypic evolution in minimal medium is consistent with at least three-fold larger propensity for mutations to alter growth rate compared to run speed.
source: This result indicates that our observed phenotypic evolution is consistent with at least three-fold larger propensity for mutations to alter growth rate compared to run speed in minimal medium (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The capacity of mutations to alter run speed or growth rate relative to founder depends on the nutrient conditions.
source: This suggests that the capacity of mutations to alter run speed or growth rate relative to founder depends on the nutrient conditions
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and inferred from the modeling analysis.

claim: Changes in the capacity for mutations to alter traits qualitatively alter the direction of evolution along a Pareto frontier.
source: and that changes in this capacity qualitatively alter the direction of evolution along a Pareto frontier (Shoval et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by modeling analysis and a citation.

claim: Mutations that can increase growth rate in rich medium are few while in minimal medium the propensity for mutations increasing growth rate is substantially larger.
source: This result captures the intuition that mutations that can increase growth rate in rich medium are few while in minimal medium the propensity for mutations increasing growth rate is substantially larger.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the modeling results.

claim: The most striking observation of the study is the divergent trajectories of phenotypic evolution shown in Figure 4a–b.
source: The most striking observation of our study is the divergent trajectories of phenotypic evolution shown in Figure 4a–b.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The evolution of faster migration results in environmentally dependent phenotypic outcomes.
source: This observation shows that the evolution of faster migration results in environmentally dependent phenotypic outcomes.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by the divergent phenotypic trajectories observed in different media.

claim: When selection pressures place demands on multiple traits simultaneously, evolution along the frontier can reflect differing genetic capacity for adaptation of each phenotype rather than simply the fitness benefit of improving each trait.
source: Our study shows that when selection pressures place demands on multiple traits simultaneously, evolution along the frontier can reflect differing genetic capacity for adaptation of each phenotype rather than simply the fitness benefit of improving each trait.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by the modeling and experimental results.

claim: The mutations observed in both rich and minimal media alter negative regulators (a protease in the case of clpX and a transcriptional repressor in the case of galS).
source: The mutations we observe in both rich and minimal media alter negative regulators (a protease in the case of clpX and a transcriptional repressor in the case of galS).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by the sequencing and reconstruction data.

claim: Microevolution is dominated by the disruption of negative regulation.
source: This supports the hypothesis that microevolution is dominated by the disruption of negative regulation (Lind et al., 2015)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by the observed mutations and a citation.

claim: The direction of phenotypic evolution can be predicted by determining where negative regulatory elements reside in genetic and proteomic networks.
source: and suggests that the direction of phenotypic evolution can be predicted by determining where negative regulatory elements reside in genetic and proteomic networks.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a hypothesis based on the results.

claim: The mutations examined appear to be more subtle than simple loss of function, since knockout mutants for both clpX and galS do not exhibit fast migration.
source: The mutations we examined appear to be more subtle than simple loss of function, since knockout mutants for both clpX and galS do not exhibit fast migration
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by experimental data comparing point mutations to knockouts.

claim: Yi and Dean selected E. coli alternately for growth in well mixed conditions and chemotaxis using a capillary assay and observed a trade-off between growth rate and swimming speed which was circumvented by phenotypic plasticity.
source: For example, Yi and Dean, 2016 selected E. coli alternately for growth in well mixed conditions and chemotaxis using a capillary assay and observed a trade-off between growth rate and swimming speed which was circumvented by phenotypic plasticity.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation.

claim: No evolution beyond the Pareto frontier was observed in this study, possibly because conditions simultaneously select for growth and motility rather than alternating between selection pressures.
source: We observe no evolution beyond the Pareto frontier in our study, possibly because our conditions simultaneously select for growth and motility rather than alternating between selection pressures.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and represents an inference from comparing results to other studies.

claim: Evolutionarily persistent trade-offs may reflect selection pressures that occur simultaneously in nature.
source: This suggests that evolutionarily persistent trade-offs may reflect selection pressures that occur simultaneously in nature.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a hypothesis based on the results.

claim: van Ditmarsch et al. and Deforet et al. selected Pseudomonas aeruginosa for a hyperswarming phenotype on hard agar.
source: In addition, van Ditmarsch et al. (2013) and Deforet et al. (2014) select Pseudomonas aeruginosa for a hyperswarming phenotype on hard agar.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: Hyperswarmers selected by van Ditmarsch et al. exhibit a decline in growth rate and swimming speed in liquid and a deficit in biofilm formation.
source: Phenotypically, hyperswarmers selected in this way exhibit a decline in growth rate and swimming speed in liquid and a deficit in biofilm formation (van Ditmarsch et al., 2013; Deforet et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: Evolved phenotypes can depend on whether selection occurs at well defined spatial locations in a structured population or through periodic removal of spatial structure.
source: In light of our study, these results suggest that evolved phenotypes can depend on whether selection occurs at well defined spatial locations in a structured population (e.g. migrating fronts) or through periodic removal of spatial structure.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference from comparing results to other studies.

claim: Both Yi and Dean and van Ditmarsch et al. observe mutations that alter regulation of motility and chemotaxis genes.
source: Interestingly, both Yi and Dean (2016) and van Ditmarsch et al. (2013) observe mutations that alter regulation of motility and chemotaxis genes.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: None of the mutations observed in this experiment were found by Yi and Dean, despite evolution along similar Pareto frontiers.
source: None of the mutations observed in our experiment were found by Yi and Dean, despite evolution along similar Pareto frontiers.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on comparison of sequencing results.

claim: Determining the allowed directions of phenotypic variation may be a more powerful approach to predicting evolution than cataloging mutations alone.
source: This suggests that determining the allowed directions of phenotypic variation may be a more powerful approach to predicting evolution than cataloging mutations alone.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a hypothesis based on the results.

claim: The mechanism of the trade-off between growth rate and swimming speed has not been determined.
source: The mechanism of the trade-off between growth rate and swimming speed has, to our knowledge, not been determined.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Over-expression of motility operons could drive the reductions in growth rate observed in rich medium.
source: However, over-expression of motility operons could drive the reductions in growth rate we observe in rich medium.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a hypothesis.

claim: Increases in speed could arise passively from reductions in cell size which reduce hydrodynamic drag.
source: Subsequent increases in speed could then arise passively from reductions in cell size which reduce hydrodynamic drag (Taheri-Araghi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a hypothesis and supported by a citation.

claim: Changes in cell size due to measured changes in growth rate could not account for the large change in swimming speed observed.
source: We could not account for the large change in swimming speed we observe through growth rate mediated changes in cell size alone (Appendix 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on calculations described in Appendix 1.

claim: To definitively characterize the mechanism of the trade-off will require measurements of cell size, gene expression, flagellar length and proton motive force.
source: To definitively characterize the mechanism of this trade-off will require measurements of cell size, gene expression, flagellar length and proton motive force.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a recommendation for future work.
